provenance.fine_print: On our July 23 call · reconstructed from the transcript, with your consent · quotes are yours, verbatim · nothing here is public, link-only. The scoring engine runs on Claude today; an internal version could run on Gemini, nothing leaving Google. Your call to open that door, or not.

hero.title: The 60-Second Read
hero.description: Our call written as a brief: the bet before, what happened after, the moment it caught, and one move.
hero.title_html: What I got right, where I was wrong, and what to do about it.
hero.lead_html: Our call, written as a brief: the same bite-size shape you already reach for, plus the one part a brief never has. The after. No math on this page. If you ever want the scoring, it's one click down, closed until you ask.

bet.sub: The bet I filed on you before the call. The same three lines your pre-brief gives you: who they are, what they want, what you want.

cards.label: Who you are
cards.head: A warm hello, no agenda.
cards.body_html: You opened with <q>nothing to sell or ask, just wanted to say kudos.</q> I filed you as a genuine fan stopping by.

cards.label: What you want
cards.head: To swap stories, maybe help.
cards.body_html: Receptive, not committed. <q>Let me know if I can help.</q> I wasn't expecting a specific ask to land.

cards.label: What I want
cards.head: An honest read, not a deal.
cards.body_html: Your head on where ARCS still reads fuzzy, and to hear how Agentum's going. Two builders, no pitch.

outcome.sub: What actually happened, scored against that bet. This is the half a normal brief never fills in.

cards.label: What happened
cards.head: You're not a fan. You're the exact user.
cards.body_html: You run the ~20-person team that builds Google's pre-meeting exec briefs. You'd already proven the thing I thought I was introducing.

cards.label: Where I was wrong
cards.head: I under-read you by a mile.
cards.body_html: I had you as warm-but-casual. You pulled hard: <q>be selfish, what do you need, I want to move you forward.</q> That's the miss, kept on purpose.

cards.label: What to do
cards.head: Show you the before/after on yourself.
cards.body_html: You said that's the magic worth showing. So here it is. And next time we talk, I lead with the practitioner, not the pitch.

spark.sub: One line on the call lit everything this page is. Your line, not mine.
spark.quote: It'd be great to see your hypothesis on me before, and what happened after our conversation. That's the magic.
spark.body_html: You didn't need convincing; you'd already lived the thesis. You automated the Sundar brief in 2020, no AI, and his mind was blown. So when you named the before-and-after as the magic, you weren't asking for a new idea. You were pointing at the one you'd proven yourself. This page is that line, built.

move.sub: One move, not a menu. Everything above is just the demo.
move.panel_html: Send me one of your upcoming meetings: a customer, a counterpart, whoever's next. I file the read before it, you run the meeting, and we score my bet against what actually happened. That's the pilot.

math.summary_label: Show the work · the bookie behind the read
math.summary_html: You said: don't show me the math, tell me what to say. Agreed, so it lives here, shut, out of your way. The simplest way to picture it: the work is a bookie. I file a bet on how the call will go, the bookie sets the line, and the call itself settles it. The line drifts toward the read the evidence backs and away from the one it doesn't. A losing bet is the point; a brief that can't be wrong can't teach you anything. Open only if you ever want the receipt.

rows.actual: Got it, plus a live user

who.h4: So, who's it for, and how would you use it
rows: The person filing the read. You, before a meeting. Or your team before a partner call.
The three cards up top are your pre-brief. The same bite-size snack you already reach for, nothing new to learn.
The cards below them are the part that's usually lost the moment the call ends. Filled in once, so the next brief starts smarter instead of from scratch.
